content: A stationary process, also referred to as a strictly stationary or strongly stationary process, is a type of stochastic process in which the joint probability distribution remains unchanged when the process is shifted in time or space. This invariance implies that statistical parameters such as the mean and variance, if they exist, remain constant over time or position. Stationarity is a critical concept in time series analysis, where raw data are often transformed to achieve stationarity. For instance, economic data frequently exhibit seasonality or dependence on price levels. Processes that can be expressed as a combination of a stationary process and one or more processes with a trend are called trend stationary. The act of transforming such data to isolate the stationary component for analysis is known as de-trending. Formally, consider a stochastic process ( X_t ), and let ( F_{X_{t_1}, ldots, X_{t_k}}(x_{t_1}, ldots, x_{t_k}) ) denote the cumulative distribution function of the joint distribution of ( X_t ) at times ( t_1, ldots, t_k ). The process ( X_t ) is defined as stationary if, for all ( k ), for all time shifts ( tau ), and for all time points ( t_1, ldots, t_k ), the joint distribution remains invariant under the time shift. An example of a stationary process is white noise, which has constant statistical properties over time. In contrast, the sound of a cymbal crash is not stationary because its acoustic power, and consequently its variance, decreases over time. Another example of a discrete-time stationary process is a Bernoulli scheme, where the random variable can take one of ( N ) possible values. Other examples include autoregressive and moving average signals. A weaker form of stationarity, often used in signal processing, is called weak-sense stationarity (WSS), wide-sense stationarity, second-order stationarity, or covariance stationarity. In this case, the process only requires that the first and second moments (mean and covariance) do not vary with time. Any strictly stationary process that has a defined mean and covariance is also WSS. For a continuous-time random process ( x(t) ) that is WSS, the following conditions must hold: 1. The mean function ( m_x(t) ) must be constant over time. 2. The correlation function must depend only on the time difference between two points, ( t_1 ) and ( t_2 ), rather than on the absolute time values. This allows the correlation function to be indexed by a single variable instead of two. For simplicity, instead of writing the correlation function in terms of two time variables, it is often abbreviated to depend on the time difference alone. When processing WSS random signals using linear, time-invariant (LTI) filters, the correlation function can be treated as a linear operator. Since this operator depends only on the time difference (making it a circulant operator), its eigenfunctions are the Fourier complex exponentials. Furthermore, because the eigenfunctions of LTI systems are also complex exponentials, the processing of WSS random signals becomes highly efficient. All computations can be performed in the frequency domain, making the WSS assumption particularly advantageous in signal processing algorithms.
